questions.topic: Kinematics - Projectile Motion (Maximum Height)
questions.q: A soccer player kicks a ball from the ground with an initial velocity $v_0 = 25\text{ m/s}$ inclined at an angle $\alpha = 20^\circ$ to the ground. What is the maximum height $h_{\max}$ reached by the ball?
questions.hint: First calculate the vertical component of velocity $v_{0y} = v_0 \sin(\alpha)$ and then use the formula for maximum height $h_{\max} = \frac{v_{0y}^2}{2g}$.
explanations: Correct! The vertical component of initial velocity is $v_{0y} = 25 \cdot \sin(20^\circ) \approx 8.55\text{ m/s}$. The maximum height is $h_{\max} = \frac{(8.55)^2}{2 \cdot 9.8} \approx \frac{73.1}{19.6} \approx 3.73\text{ m}$.
Incorrect. $8.55\text{ m/s}$ is the value of the vertical component of initial velocity $v_{0y}$, not the maximum height.
Incorrect. Error in calculating the denominator (failed to divide by 2).

questions.topic: Kinematics - Projectile Motion (Range)
questions.q: For the same kick ($v_0 = 25\text{ m/s}$, $\alpha = 20^\circ$), what is the range $R$ of the ball?
questions.hint: Use the range formula $R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin(2\alpha)}{g}$.
explanations: Correct! $R = \frac{25^2 \cdot \sin(40^\circ)}{9.8} = \frac{625 \cdot 0.6428}{9.8} \approx \frac{401.7}{9.8} \approx 41\text{ m}$.
Incorrect. $25\text{ m}$ corresponds to the magnitude of initial velocity in m/s, not the range.
Incorrect. Error in applying the double-angle formula or in the value of $\sin(40^\circ)$.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Initial Velocity Components
questions.q: A tennis player hits a ball at an angle of $45^\circ$ to the ground with an initial velocity $v_0 = 21\text{ m/s}$. What are the horizontal $v_{0x}$ and vertical $v_{0y}$ components of the initial velocity?
questions.hint: At an angle of $45^\circ$, the two components are equal and equal $v_0 \cos(45^\circ) = v_0 \sin(45^\circ)$.
explanations: Correct! Since $\cos(45^\circ) = \sin(45^\circ) \approx 0.7071$, the components are $v_{0x} = v_{0y} = 21 \cdot 0.7071 \approx 14.85\text{ m/s} \approx 15\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. These would be the components for a completely horizontal launch.
Incorrect. $10.5\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by mistakenly dividing by $2$ instead of multiplying by $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Range at a 45-Degree Angle
questions.q: For the tennis ball hit at $v_0 = 21\text{ m/s}$ at an angle of $45^\circ$, calculate the range $R$.
questions.hint: At an angle of $45^\circ$, the range is maximum and given by $R = \frac{v_0^2}{g}$ (or $R = \frac{2 v_{0x} v_{0y}}{g}$ using approximate values).
explanations: Correct! Using approximate components $v_{0x} = v_{0y} \approx 15\text{ m/s}$: $R = \frac{2 \cdot 15 \cdot 15}{9.8} = \frac{450}{9.8} \approx 45.9\text{ m} \approx 46\text{ m}$ (or with the exact formula $R = \frac{21^2}{9.8} \approx 45\text{ m}$).
Incorrect. $21\text{ m}$ is the initial speed magnitude, not the distance traveled.
Incorrect. This would be obtained by mistakenly doubling the range.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Horizontal Launch and Final Velocity
questions.q: A ball is launched horizontally from a height $h = 12\text{ m}$. Knowing that the speed with which it hits the ground is twice the initial speed ($v_{\text{imp}} = 2 v_0$), what is the initial velocity $v_0$?
questions.hint: Relate vertical velocity $v_y = \sqrt{2gh}$ to total velocity $v_{\text{imp}}^2 = v_0^2 + v_y^2 = 4v_0^2$, yielding $3v_0^2 = 2gh$.
explanations: Correct! Vertical velocity at impact is $v_y = \sqrt{2 g h} \approx \sqrt{2 \cdot 9.8 \cdot 12} \approx 15.3\text{ m/s}$. Since $v_{\text{imp}}^2 = v_0^2 + v_y^2$ and $v_{\text{imp}} = 2 v_0$, we get $4 v_0^2 = v_0^2 + v_y^2 \implies 3 v_0^2 = v_y^2 \implies v_0 = \frac{v_y}{\sqrt{3}} \approx \frac{15.3}{1.732} \approx 8.83\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $15.3\text{ m/s}$ is only the vertical component $v_y$ of velocity upon impact.
Incorrect. Calculation error resulting from incorrectly halving the result.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Projectile Motion (Jumping the Ditch)
questions.q: A motorcycle travels at $54\text{ km/h}$ when encountering a $3\text{ m}$ wide ditch with a $1\text{ m}$ height difference between the two edges. If the rider launches horizontally, will they reach the other side or fall into the ditch?
questions.hint: First convert speed to $\text{m/s}$ ($v_0 = 15\text{ m/s}$). Calculate fall time for the $1\text{ m}$ height difference with $t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$ and determine the horizontal distance covered $x = v_0 \cdot t$.
options: Yes, because it covers about $6.78\text{ m}$ horizontally, well exceeding the $3\text{ m}$ ditch.
No, because it covers only $2.25\text{ m}$ and falls into the ditch.
No, the speed of $54\text{ km/h}$ is insufficient to leave the edge.
explanations: Correct! Initial speed in m/s is $v_0 = \frac{54}{3.6} = 15\text{ m/s}$. Time needed to drop $h = 1\text{ m}$ is $t = \sqrt{\frac{2 \cdot 1}{9.8}} \approx 0.452\text{ s}$. Horizontal distance covered is $x = 15 \cdot 0.452 \approx 6.78\text{ m}$. Since $6.78\text{ m} > 3\text{ m}$, the rider lands beyond the ditch.
Incorrect. $2.25\text{ m}$ would be obtained by incorrectly calculating time or using speed in km/h without converting it.
Incorrect. At $15\text{ m/s}$, the motorcycle has enough momentum to clear the ditch width.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Projectile Motion (Cliff Diver Flight Time)
questions.q: An Acapulco cliff diver jumps horizontally from a height of $35\text{ m}$. What is their flight time $t$ before touching the water? (Use $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.hint: In projectile motion, vertical fall follows $h = \frac{1}{2} g t^2 \implies t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$.
explanations: Correct! $t = \sqrt{\frac{2 \cdot 35}{9.8}} = \sqrt{\frac{70}{9.8}} = \sqrt{7.143} \approx 2.67\text{ s}$.
Incorrect. $3.57\text{ s}$ would be obtained by forgetting to multiply $h$ by $2$ inside the square root or dividing by an incorrect $g$ value.
Incorrect. Calculation error when taking the square root.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Projectile Motion (Minimum Safe Velocity)
questions.q: Knowing that rocks extend $5\text{ m}$ from the base of the platform ($h = 35\text{ m}$, flight time $t = 2.67\text{ s}$), what is the minimum horizontal velocity $v_{\min}$ that allows the diver to clear the rocks?
questions.hint: Horizontally, motion is uniform linear: $d = v_{\min} \cdot t \implies v_{\min} = \frac{d}{t}$.
explanations: Correct! To cover horizontal distance $d = 5\text{ m}$ during flight time $t = 2.67\text{ s}$, minimum horizontal velocity must be $v_{\min} = \frac{d}{t} = \frac{5\text{ m}}{2.67\text{ s}} \approx 1.87\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $3.74\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by mistakenly doubling the required speed.
Incorrect. $0.53\text{ m/s}$ is the reciprocal of speed or a division error ($2.67 / 5$).

questions.topic: Kinematics - Projectile Motion from Elevation (Max Height and Flight Time)
questions.q: A ball is kicked with an initial velocity $v_0 = 10\text{ m/s}$ at an angle $\theta = 30^\circ$ from the top of a $h_0 = 32\text{ m}$ tall building. Calculate the maximum height $h_{\max}$ reached and the flight time $t_{\text{flight}}$.
questions.hint: Vertical velocity component is $v_{0y} = v_0 \sin(30^\circ) = 5\text{ m/s}$. Maximum height above ground is $h_{\max} = h_0 + \frac{v_{0y}^2}{2g}$, while flight time is obtained by setting $y(t) = 0$.
explanations: Correct! $v_{0y} = 10 \cdot \sin(30^\circ) = 5\text{ m/s}$. Maximum height is $h_{\max} = 32 + \frac{5^2}{2 \cdot 9.81} = 32 + 1.27 = 33.28\text{ m}$. Solving $-4.905 t^2 + 5t + 32 = 0$ yields $t_{\text{flight}} \approx 3.12\text{ s}$.
Incorrect. $32\text{ m}$ does not account for the additional altitude reached above the building during the first phase of flight.
Incorrect. Results from incorrectly adding total kinetic energy or using total speed $10\text{ m/s}$ instead of vertical component $v_{0y}$.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Projectile Motion from Elevation (Range and Final Speed)
questions.q: For the same ball kicked from the building ($v_0 = 10\text{ m/s}$, $\theta = 30^\circ$, $h_0 = 32\text{ m}$, $t_{\text{flight}} = 3.12\text{ s}$), determine range $R$ from the building base and final speed magnitude $v_{\text{final}}$ upon hitting the ground.
questions.hint: Horizontal velocity is $v_x = v_0 \cos(30^\circ) \approx 8.66\text{ m/s}$. Range is $R = v_x \cdot t_{\text{flight}}$. For final speed, use conservation of energy: $v_{\text{final}} = \sqrt{v_0^2 + 2 g h_0}$.
explanations: Correct! Horizontal component is $v_x = 10 \cdot \cos(30^\circ) \approx 8.66\text{ m/s}$. Thus range is $R = 8.66 \cdot 3.12 \approx 27.02\text{ m}$. For impact speed: $v_{\text{final}} = \sqrt{10^2 + 2 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 32} = \sqrt{100 + 627.84} = \sqrt{727.84} \approx 27.01\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $31.20\text{ m}$ would be obtained by multiplying flight time by total speed $10\text{ m/s}$ instead of horizontal component $v_x$.
Incorrect. Error in trigonometric decomposition of initial velocity.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Uniform Circular Motion
questions.q: A particle moves along a circle of radius $r = 15\text{ m}$ at constant tangential speed $v = 25\text{ m/s}$. Calculate period $T$, frequency $f$, centripetal acceleration $a_c$, and angular velocity $\omega$.
questions.hint: Use formulas: $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v}$, $f = \frac{1}{T}$, $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$, and $\omega = \frac{v}{r}$.
explanations: Correct! $T = \frac{2 \pi \cdot 15}{25} \approx 3.77\text{ s}$; $f = \frac{1}{3.77} \approx 0.27\text{ Hz}$; $a_c = \frac{25^2}{15} = \frac{625}{15} \approx 41.67\text{ m/s}^2$; $\omega = \frac{25}{15} \approx 1.67\text{ rad/s}$.
Incorrect. Swapped values between period and angular velocity.
Incorrect. Error in calculating frequency (factor of 10) and centripetal acceleration.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Circular Orbits and Satellites
questions.q: An artificial satellite orbiting Earth experiences centripetal acceleration $a_c = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$. Considering orbit radius equal to Earth's radius $r = 6371\text{ km}$, calculate tangential velocity $v$ and orbital period $T$.
questions.hint: Convert $r$ to meters ($6371000\text{ m}$). From centripetal acceleration $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$, find $v = \sqrt{a_c \cdot r}$. Then find $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v}$ and convert to minutes.
explanations: Correct! $v = \sqrt{9.8 \cdot 6371000} = \sqrt{62435800} \approx 7902\text{ m/s}$ (about $7.9\text{ km/s}$). Period is $T = \frac{2 \pi \cdot 6371000}{7902} \approx 5066\text{ s}$. Dividing by $60$ gives $T \approx 84.4\text{ min}$.
Incorrect. $62435$ is $v^2$ before taking the square root.
Incorrect. $5066$ is the period expressed in seconds, not minutes.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Earth's Orbital Motion
questions.q: Calculate tangential speed magnitude $v$ of Earth in its revolution around the Sun, given Earth's orbital radius $r = 1.49 \cdot 10^{11}\text{ m}$.
questions.hint: Earth's revolution period is one year ($1\text{ year} \approx 365.25\text{ days} \approx 3.156 \cdot 10^7\text{ s}$). Apply formula $v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}$.
explanations: Correct! One year lasts $T = 365.25 \cdot 24 \cdot 3600 \approx 3.156 \cdot 10^7\text{ s}$. Orbital speed is $v = \frac{2\pi \cdot 1.49 \cdot 10^{11}}{3.156 \cdot 10^7} \approx 2.95 \cdot 10^4\text{ m/s}$ (about $29.5\text{ km/s}$).
Incorrect. Order of magnitude error due to incorrect conversion from days to seconds.
Incorrect. Corresponds to a calculation confusing gravitational acceleration with orbital velocity.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Circular Motion (Go-Kart Chase)
questions.q: On a circular go-kart track with radius $R = 40\text{ m}$, two participants start at the same moment from opposite ends of a diameter. The second travels at constant speed $V_B = 40\text{ km/h}$. What speed $V_A$ must the first driver maintain to catch the second after the second completes $2.5$ laps, and how long does it take?
questions.hint: The second driver covers $2.5$ circumferences: $d_B = 2.5 \cdot (2\pi R)$. Located at opposite diameter end (half lap behind), the first driver must cover $d_A = 3.0 \cdot (2\pi R)$ in the same time. Speed is proportional to distance covered.
explanations: Correct! Converting speed $V_B = 40\text{ km/h} \approx 11.11\text{ m/s}$ and distance $d_B = 2.5 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 40 \approx 628.32\text{ m}$, time taken is $t = \frac{d_B}{V_B} \approx 56.58\text{ s}$. Since first driver must make $3$ laps in same time, speed is $V_A = V_B \cdot \frac{3}{2.5} = 40 \cdot 1.2 = 48\text{ km/h}$.
Incorrect. $50\text{ km/h}$ assumes first driver covers distance greater than $3$ laps.
Incorrect. If $V_A = V_B$, distance between them stays constant (half lap gap) and no overtake occurs.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Uniform Circular Motion (Hour and Minute Hands)
questions.q: A clock has three hands: hour hand ($1\text{ cm}$ long) and minute hand ($1.4\text{ cm}$ long). Determine period $T$, angular velocity $\omega$, and tangential velocity $v$ at the tip of each hand.
questions.hint: Hour hand period is $T_{\text{hour}} = 12\text{ h} = 43200\text{ s}$, minute hand is $T_{\text{min}} = 1\text{ h} = 3600\text{ s}$. Use $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ and $v = \omega \cdot r$.
options: Hour: $T = 43200\text{ s}$, $\omega \approx 1.45 \cdot 10^{-4}\text{ rad/s}$, $v \approx 1.45 \cdot 10^{-6}\text{ m/s}$; Minute: $T = 3600\text{ s}$, $\omega \approx 1.75 \cdot 10^{-3}\text{ rad/s}$, $v \approx 2.45 \cdot 10^{-5}\text{ m/s}$

Hour: $T = 86400\text{ s}$, $\omega \approx 7.27 \cdot 10^{-5}\text{ rad/s}$, $v \approx 7.27 \cdot 10^{-7}\text{ m/s}$; Minute: $T = 3600\text{ s}$, $\omega \approx 1.75 \cdot 10^{-3}\text{ rad/s}$, $v \approx 2.45 \cdot 10^{-5}\text{ m/s}$

Hour: $T = 43200\text{ s}$, $\omega \approx 1.45 \cdot 10^{-4}\text{ rad/s}$, $v \approx 1.45 \cdot 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}$; Minute: $T = 60\text{ s}$, $\omega \approx 0.105\text{ rad/s}$, $v \approx 1.47 \cdot 10^{-3}\text{ m/s}$
explanations: Correct! Hour hand: $T = 43200\text{ s}$, $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{43200} \approx 1.45 \cdot 10^{-4}\text{ rad/s}$, $v = \omega \cdot 0.01\text{ m} \approx 1.45 \cdot 10^{-6}\text{ m/s}$. Minute hand: $T = 3600\text{ s}$, $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{3600} \approx 1.75 \cdot 10^{-3}\text{ rad/s}$, $v = \omega \cdot 0.014\text{ m} \approx 2.45 \cdot 10^{-5}\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. Hour hand period on analog clock is 12 hours ($43200\text{ s}$), not 24 hours ($86400\text{ s}$).
Incorrect. Conversion error in periods or hand lengths from centimeters to meters.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Uniform Circular Motion (Second Hand)
questions.q: Considering the second hand ($1.6\text{ cm}$ long) of the same clock, calculate period $T$, angular velocity $\omega$, tangential velocity $v$, and centripetal acceleration $a_c$ at its tip.
questions.hint: Second hand completes full revolution in $T = 60\text{ s}$. Use $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$, $v = \omega \cdot r$, and $a_c = \omega^2 \cdot r$.
explanations: Correct! $T = 60\text{ s}$; $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{60} \approx 0.105\text{ rad/s}$; $v = 0.105 \cdot 0.016\text{ m} \approx 1.68 \cdot 10^{-3}\text{ m/s}$; $a_c = (0.105)^2 \cdot 0.016 \approx 1.76 \cdot 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}^2$.
Incorrect. Values of angular velocity and acceleration incorrectly correspond to minute hand scale.
Incorrect. Second hand period is 60 seconds, not 1 second.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Uniform Circular Motion (Turntable)
questions.q: A vinyl record on a turntable rotates at $33$ revolutions per minute ($33\text{ rpm}$). Calculate period $T$, frequency $f$, and angular velocity $\omega$.
questions.hint: Frequency is revolutions per second: $f = \frac{33}{60}\text{ Hz}$. Period is $T = \frac{1}{f}$ and angular velocity is $\omega = 2\pi f$.
explanations: Correct! $f = \frac{33}{60} = 0.55\text{ Hz}$; $T = \frac{1}{0.55} \approx 1.82\text{ s}$; $\omega = 2\pi \cdot 0.55 \approx 3.46\text{ rad/s}$.
Incorrect. Swapped values between period and frequency.
Incorrect. Inverted definition of rotational frequency.

questions.topic: Kinematics - Simple Harmonic Motion
questions.q: In simple harmonic motion of a particle, maximum acceleration is $a_{\max} = 2.5\text{ m/s}^2$ and oscillation period is $T = 1.2\text{ s}$. Determine frequency $f$, amplitude $A$, and maximum speed $v_{\max}$.
questions.hint: Frequency is $f = \frac{1}{T}$. Angular frequency is $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$. Find amplitude from $a_{\max} = \omega^2 A$ and maximum speed from $v_{\max} = \omega A$.
explanations: Correct! $f = \frac{1}{1.2} \approx 0.83\text{ Hz}$. Angular frequency is $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{1.2} \approx 5.24\text{ rad/s}$. Amplitude is $A = \frac{a_{\max}}{\omega^2} = \frac{2.5}{(5.24)^2} \approx 0.091\text{ m} = 9.1\text{ cm} \approx 9\text{ cm}$. Maximum speed is $v_{\max} = \omega A = 5.24 \cdot 0.091 \approx 0.47\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. Confuses frequency with period and calculates incorrect amplitude and speed.
Incorrect. Error calculating $\omega^2$ in denominator when solving for amplitude.

questions.topic: Dynamics - Newton's Second Law
questions.q: A force of $15\text{ N}$ applied to a body of mass $m$ causes it to move along a straight line, increasing speed by $10\text{ m/s}$ every $2\text{ s}$. Determine mass $m$ of the body.
questions.hint: First calculate constant acceleration using $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$, then apply Newton's Second Law $F = m \cdot a$.
explanations: Correct! Acceleration is $a = \frac{10\text{ m/s}}{2\text{ s}} = 5\text{ m/s}^2$. Applying $F = m \cdot a$, we get $m = \frac{F}{a} = \frac{15\text{ N}}{5\text{ m/s}^2} = 3\text{ kg}$.
Incorrect. $7.5\text{ kg}$ is obtained by dividing force directly by velocity change $\Delta v$ without considering time.
Incorrect. Calculation error in division between force and acceleration.

questions.topic: Dynamics - Hooke's Law and Static Equilibrium
questions.q: A spring has a spring constant $k = 0.5\text{ N/cm}$. If a weight is suspended from the spring, it stretches by $3.5\text{ cm}$. What is the mass of the suspended object?
questions.hint: Use Hooke's law $F_e = k \cdot x$ to determine spring force, which at equilibrium balances weight force $F_p = m \cdot g$.
explanations: Correct! Spring force exerted is $F_e = k \cdot x = 0.5\text{ N/cm} \cdot 3.5\text{ cm} = 1.75\text{ N}$. At equilibrium $F_p = F_e$, so $m = \frac{F_e}{g} = \frac{1.75\text{ N}}{9.81\text{ m/s}^2} \approx 0.178\text{ kg} \approx 180\text{ g}$.
Incorrect. $175\text{ g}$ directly confuses spring force value in Newtons ($1.75\text{ N}$) with mass without dividing by $g$.
Incorrect. Calculation error in spring constant units or stretch.

questions.topic: Dynamics - Newton's First Law and Friction
questions.q: A car engine provides a driving force of $300\text{ N}$ while traveling at constant speed. Can there be a friction force acting on the car in this case? If so, what is its magnitude?
questions.hint: Remember Newton's First Law: if a body moves at constant speed, acceleration is zero and net external force must be zero.
options: Yes, there is a friction force with magnitude $300\text{ N}$
No, there is no friction force because the car moves at constant speed
Yes, there is a friction force, but its magnitude is less than $300\text{ N}$
explanations: Correct! If car proceeds at constant velocity, acceleration is zero and net force is zero ($F_{\text{net}} = 0$). Consequently, driving force must balance opposing friction force: $F_{\text{friction}} = F_{\text{driving}} = 300\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. If there were no friction and $300\text{ N}$ driving force were applied, car would accelerate instead of maintaining constant speed.
Incorrect. If friction were less than $300\text{ N}$, net forward force would cause car to accelerate.

questions.topic: Dynamics - Harmonic Oscillator (Maximum Speed)
questions.q: A mass $m = 200\text{ g}$ oscillates horizontally without friction at the end of a spring with $k = 7.0\text{ N/m}$. If mass is displaced $5.0\text{ cm}$ from equilibrium and released, what is its maximum speed?
questions.hint: Maximum speed in harmonic motion is reached when passing equilibrium ($x=0$) and equals $v_{\max} = \omega \cdot A$, with $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$.
explanations: Correct! Angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{7.0\text{ N/m}}{0.2\text{ kg}}} \approx 5.916\text{ rad/s}$. Amplitude is $A = 0.05\text{ m}$. Maximum speed is $v_{\max} = \omega \cdot A \approx 5.916 \cdot 0.05 \approx 0.296\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $0.237\text{ m/s}$ is intermediate speed when mass is $3.0\text{ cm}$ from equilibrium.
Incorrect. Calculation error converting mass to kilograms.

questions.topic: Dynamics - Harmonic Oscillator (Speed at Position)
questions.q: For a harmonic oscillator with mass $m = 200\text{ g}$, stiffness $k = 7.0\text{ N/m}$, and amplitude $A = 5.0\text{ cm}$, what is the speed of the mass when located at $3.0\text{ cm}$ from equilibrium?
questions.hint: Use relationship $v(x) = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$ or mechanical energy conservation $E = \frac{1}{2} k A^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} k x^2$.
explanations: Correct! For $x = 0.03\text{ m}$, $\sqrt{A^2 - x^2} = \sqrt{0.05^2 - 0.03^2} = 0.04\text{ m}$. Speed is $v = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} = 5.916 \cdot 0.04 \approx 0.237\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. Value corresponds to maximum speed at center of oscillation ($x=0$).
Incorrect. Calculation error in difference of squares under root.

questions.topic: Dynamics - Harmonic Oscillator (Acceleration)
questions.q: For the same oscillating system ($m = 200\text{ g}$, $k = 7.0\text{ N/m}$, amplitude $A = 5.0\text{ cm}$), what are acceleration magnitudes at equilibrium ($x = 0$) and at distance $x = 3.0\text{ cm}$?
questions.hint: Acceleration in harmonic motion varies proportionally to displacement: $a(x) = \omega^2 x = \frac{k}{m} x$.
explanations: Correct! At equilibrium ($x = 0$) spring force is zero, so $a(0) = 0\text{ m/s}^2$. For $x = 0.03\text{ m}$, acceleration is $a = \frac{k}{m} x = \frac{7.0}{0.2} \cdot 0.03 = 35 \cdot 0.03 = 1.05\text{ m/s}^2$.
Incorrect. Swapped acceleration values between equilibrium and $3.0\text{ cm}$ point.
Incorrect. $1.75\text{ m/s}^2$ is maximum acceleration at maximum amplitude ($x = 5.0\text{ cm}$).

questions.topic: Dynamics - Separation in Simple Harmonic Motion
questions.q: In an engine, a piston undergoes simple harmonic motion with amplitude $y_0 = 7\text{ cm}$. If a washer rests on top of the piston and engine speed is slowly increased, at what frequency will washer lose contact with piston?
questions.hint: Washer loses contact when downward harmonic acceleration exceeds gravitational acceleration $g$, i.e., $a_{\max} = \omega^2 y_0 = g$.
explanations: Correct! Separation occurs when maximum piston acceleration equals $g$: $\omega^2 y_0 = g \implies \omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{y_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{9.81}{0.07}} \approx 11.84\text{ rad/s}$. Threshold frequency is $f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{11.84}{2\pi} \approx 1.88\text{ Hz}$.
Incorrect. Factor of $2$ error due to incorrect calculation relating angular frequency.
Incorrect. Error converting amplitude $y_0$ from centimeters to meters.

questions.topic: Dynamics - Harmonic Oscillator (Spring Constant)
questions.q: A mass $m = 50\text{ g}$ oscillates with simple harmonic motion at end of frictionless horizontal spring. If amplitude $x_0 = 12\text{ cm}$ and period $T = 1.70\text{ s}$, what is spring constant $k$?
questions.hint: First calculate angular frequency $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$, then determine spring constant $k = m \cdot \omega^2$ converting mass to $\text{kg}$ ($0.05\text{ kg}$).
explanations: Correct! Angular frequency is $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{1.70} \approx 3.696\text{ rad/s}$. Spring constant is $k = m \cdot \omega^2 = 0.05 \cdot (3.696)^2 \approx 0.683\text{ N/m} \approx 0.68\text{ N/m}$.
Incorrect. Doubled value from squaring angular frequency or mass incorrectly.
Incorrect. Corresponds to half correct $k$ value.
Incorrect. $3.69$ is angular frequency $\omega$ in $\text{rad/s}$, not spring constant.

questions.topic: Dynamics - Harmonic Oscillator (Maximum Speed)
questions.q: Using same data ($m = 50\text{ g}$, $x_0 = 12\text{ cm}$, $T = 1.70\text{ s}$), determine maximum speed $v_{\max}$ reached by mass.
questions.hint: Maximum speed of harmonic oscillator is reached at equilibrium position and given by $v_{\max} = \omega \cdot x_0$.
explanations: Correct! With $\omega \approx 3.696\text{ rad/s}$ and $x_0 = 0.12\text{ m}$, maximum speed is $v_{\max} = \omega \cdot x_0 = 3.696 \cdot 0.12 \approx 0.4435\text{ m/s} \approx 0.44\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. Factor of $2$ error in amplitude or angular frequency calculation.
Incorrect. Corresponds to considering half amplitude ($6\text{ cm}$) instead of total amplitude $x_0 = 12\text{ cm}$.
Incorrect. Conversion error converting amplitude from centimeters to meters.

questions.topic: Dynamics - Harmonic Oscillator (Acceleration at Position)
questions.q: For same oscillating mass ($m = 50\text{ g}$, $x_0 = 12\text{ cm}$, $T = 1.70\text{ s}$), calculate acceleration magnitude when mass is at position $x = 6\text{ cm}$.
questions.hint: Acceleration in harmonic motion varies proportionally to position: $a = \omega^2 \cdot x$.
explanations: Correct! Since $\omega^2 = (3.696)^2 \approx 13.66\text{ rad}^2/\text{s}^2$, acceleration at position $x = 0.06\text{ m}$ is $a = \omega^2 \cdot x = 13.66 \cdot 0.06 \approx 0.82\text{ m/s}^2$.
Incorrect. $1.64\text{ m/s}^2$ is maximum acceleration at oscillation endpoints ($x = 12\text{ cm}$).
Incorrect. Calculated by incorrectly halving angular frequency.
Incorrect. Error in mass usage or squaring $\omega$.

questions.topic: Dynamics - Oscillation Period and Hooke's Law
questions.q: A mass $M = 5\text{ kg}$ suspended from a spring of negligible mass stretches it by $l = 20\text{ cm}$. If $M$ is replaced by another mass $m = 100\text{ g}$ and spring oscillates, what is period $T$ of oscillations?
questions.hint: From initial static equilibrium $M g = k l$, obtain spring constant $k = \frac{M g}{l}$. Then calculate period with new mass: $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$.
explanations: Correct! Spring constant is $k = \frac{M g}{l} = \frac{5 \cdot 9.81}{0.20} = 245.25\text{ N/m}$. Period with mass $m = 0.1\text{ kg}$ is $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{0.1}{245.25}} \approx 0.127\text{ s}$.
Incorrect. $0.897\text{ s}$ is period obtained keeping initial $5\text{ kg}$ mass instead of replacing with $100\text{ g}$.
Incorrect. Factor of $2$ error from forgetting to divide by $2$ under root or incorrectly multiplying by $\pi$.
Incorrect. Results from forgetting square root in period formula for harmonic oscillator.

questions.topic: Dynamics - Oscillations of System with Parallel Springs
questions.q: A $1300\text{ kg}$ car rests on four identical parallel springs, each with spring constant $k = 20000\text{ N/m}$. If two people with total mass $160\text{ kg}$ are inside, determine car oscillation frequency $f$, neglecting damping.
questions.hint: Total system mass is $m_{\text{tot}} = 1300 + 160 = 1460\text{ kg}$. Equivalent spring constant of four parallel springs is $k_{\text{eq}} = 4k = 80000\text{ N/m}$. Use $f = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{k_{\text{eq}}}{m_{\text{tot}}}}$.
explanations: Correct! Total mass is $m_{\text{tot}} = 1460\text{ kg}$ and equivalent spring constant is $k_{\text{eq}} = 4 \cdot 20000 = 80000\text{ N/m}$. Frequency is $f = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{80000}{1460}} = \frac{\sqrt{54.79}}{2\pi} \approx 1.18\text{ Hz}$.
Incorrect. $0.59\text{ Hz}$ would be obtained considering only one spring instead of four parallel chassis springs.
Incorrect. $2.36\text{ Hz}$ would be obtained omitting two passengers ($160\text{ kg}$) or doubling frequency.
Incorrect. Calculation error taking square root of ratio $\frac{k}{m}$.

questions.topic: Theory of Dynamics - Newton's First Law (Inertia)
questions.q: True or False?\nIf the resultant of external forces acting on a body is zero, the body remains at rest or continues to move with uniform linear motion.
questions.hint: Consider Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia).
explanations: Correct! This is the exact statement of Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia).
Incorrect. In the absence of net forces, acceleration is zero ($a = 0$), meaning vector velocity remains constant over time (body stays at rest or moves at constant speed along a straight line).

questions.topic: Theory of Dynamics - Mass and Weight
questions.q: True or False?\nThe mass of a body varies depending on local gravitational acceleration (e.g., varies between Earth and Moon).
questions.hint: Distinguish mass (intrinsic property of matter) from weight (gravitational force).
explanations: Incorrect. Mass is an intrinsic scalar quantity measuring inertia and does not change when moving body across universe.
Correct! Mass is an intrinsic property of matter and remains constant everywhere. Weight force ($F_p = m \cdot g$) varies depending on local gravitational field $g$.

questions.topic: Theory of Dynamics - Newton's Third Law (Action and Reaction)
questions.q: True or False?\nAction and reaction forces in Newton's Third Law apply to the same body and therefore always cancel each other out.
questions.hint: Think about which distinct bodies the two forces act on when pushing an object (e.g., your hands on object vs object on hands).
explanations: Incorrect. If two forces acted on same body, their sum would always be zero and no object could ever accelerate!
Correct! Action and reaction forces have equal magnitude and opposite direction, but act on two DIFFERENT bodies, which is why they never cancel on a single body.

questions.topic: Theory of Dynamics - Sliding Friction
questions.q: True or False?\nThe static friction coefficient between two contacting surfaces is generally greater than or equal to the kinetic friction coefficient.
questions.hint: Recall whether setting stationary object in motion requires more force than keeping it sliding once moving.
explanations: Correct! Because initial microscopic adhesion must be overcome to move resting body, almost always $\mu_s \ge \mu_d$.
Incorrect. Starting movement from rest requires higher threshold force than maintaining sliding.

questions.topic: Theory of Dynamics - Centripetal Force
questions.q: True or False?\nIn uniform circular motion, centripetal force changes the magnitude of velocity vector.
questions.hint: What is the effect on speed of a constant force acting perpendicularly to displacement at all times?
explanations: Incorrect. Force perpendicular to displacement does no work and does not change kinetic energy, so speed remains constant.
Correct! Centripetal force is always perpendicular to tangential velocity; thus it changes only the DIRECTION of velocity vector, leaving magnitude unchanged.

questions.topic: Theory of Dynamics - Units of Force
questions.q: In the International System of Units (SI), what fundamental units equal one Newton ($1\text{ N}$)?
questions.hint: Use Newton's Second Law formula: $F = m \cdot a$.
explanations: Correct! From $F = m \cdot a$, since mass is measured in $\text{kg}$ and acceleration in $\text{m/s}^2$, $1\text{ N} = 1\text{ kg} \cdot \text{m/s}^2$.
Incorrect. $\text{kg} \cdot \text{m/s}$ is unit of momentum ($p = m \cdot v$).
Incorrect. $\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$ corresponds to Joule ($\text{J}$), unit of work and energy.

questions.topic: Theory of Dynamics - Non-Inertial Frames and Apparent Weight
questions.q: An elevator accelerates upward with constant acceleration $a$. What is apparent weight force $F_p'$ felt by a person of mass $m$ inside?
questions.hint: In non-inertial elevator frame, downward fictitious force of $m \cdot a$ acts.
explanations: Correct! When elevator accelerates upward ($a > 0$), normal force from floor must counteract gravity and provide acceleration push: $N = m(g + a)$, making person feel heavier.
Incorrect. $m(g - a)$ is apparent weight felt when elevator accelerates downward.
Incorrect. $m \cdot g$ is real weight measured only if elevator is stationary or moving at constant speed.

questions.topic: Theory of Dynamics - Hooke's Law
questions.q: According to Hooke's Law ($F = k \cdot x$), if stretch $x$ of ideal spring is doubled, how does magnitude of restoring force change?
questions.hint: Hooke's law establishes direct proportionality between restoring force and displacement from equilibrium.
explanations: Correct! Since elastic force is directly proportional to stretch $x$, doubling $x$ doubles elastic force magnitude.
Incorrect. Elastic potential energy ($E_p = \frac{1}{2}k x^2$) quadruples, not force.
Incorrect. Restoring force depends directly on displacement, varying with stretch.

questions.topic: Theory of Dynamics - Centripetal Force
questions.q: In uniform circular motion, in which direction is centripetal force vector always pointed?
questions.hint: Analyze etymology of 'centripetal' (from Latin, 'center-seeking').
options: Toward the center of circular trajectory
explanations: Correct! Centripetal force is always directed along radius toward circle center, generating centripetal acceleration needed to curve.
Incorrect. Tangential direction is where velocity vector lies.
Incorrect. Outward direction is where centrifugal force would act, which is a fictitious force felt only inside rotating non-inertial reference frame.

questions.topic: Theory of Dynamics - Inertial Reference Frames
questions.q: What is an inertial reference frame?
questions.hint: Consider in which reference frames Newton's three laws hold strictly without needing fictitious forces.
options: A reference frame in which Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia) holds
A reference frame rotating at constant angular velocity relative to fixed stars
A reference frame undergoing constant non-zero acceleration relative to fixed frame
explanations: Correct! An inertial frame is by definition one where Law of Inertia holds. Any frame at rest or uniform linear motion relative to it is also inertial.
Incorrect. Rotating frame possesses centripetal acceleration, so non-inertial and displays fictitious forces.
Incorrect. Frame accelerating relative to inertial frame is non-inertial by definition.

questions.topic: Rotational Dynamics - Torque of a Force
questions.q: A child of mass $m = 40\text{ kg}$ is swinging on a swing. The seat is $r = 2\text{ m}$ from pivot point. Assuming child's mass is concentrated at center, determine weight force torque magnitude $M$ when swing forms angle $\theta = 30^\circ$ relative to vertical.
questions.hint: Weight force torque is given by $M = F_p \cdot r \cdot \sin(\theta)$, where $F_p = m \cdot g$ is child weight force with $g \approx 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.
explanations: Correct! Child weight force is $F_p = m \cdot g = 40 \cdot 9.8 = 392\text{ N}$. Applying vector torque formula $M = F_p \cdot r \cdot \sin(30^\circ)$, $M = 392 \cdot 2 \cdot 0.5 = 392\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
Incorrect. $784\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ obtained forgetting to multiply by $\sin(30^\circ) = 0.5$.
Incorrect. $679\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ comes from incorrect cosine usage $\cos(30^\circ) \approx 0.866$ instead of sine.
Incorrect. $196\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ obtained by further dividing result by two.
Incorrect. $80\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ obtained multiplying mass by distance without gravity acceleration $g$.

questions.topic: Rigid Body Statics - Force Couple and Torque
questions.q: To open a circular valve on a pipeline, a force couple of $F_1 = 24\text{ N}$ is applied. Given valve radius $r = 50\text{ mm}$, calculate lever arm $b_2$ of another equal-torque force couple with force magnitude $F_2 = 8\text{ N}$.
questions.hint: First couple arm is valve diameter $b_1 = 2r = 100\text{ mm} = 0.1\text{ m}$. Torque is $M = F_1 \cdot b_1$. Equating torques gives $b_2 = \frac{M}{F_2}$.
explanations: Correct! Valve arm is diameter $b_1 = 2 \cdot 50\text{ mm} = 100\text{ mm} = 0.1\text{ m}$. Torque is $M = F_1 \cdot b_1 = 24 \cdot 0.1 = 2.4\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. For second couple: $b_2 = \frac{M}{F_2} = \frac{2.4}{8} = 0.3\text{ m} = 300\text{ mm}$.
Incorrect. $150\text{ mm}$ obtained incorrectly using radius $50\text{ mm}$ as lever arm instead of diameter.
Incorrect. $600\text{ mm}$ comes from incorrectly doubling calculated lever arm.
Incorrect. $100\text{ mm}$ is initial arm $b_1$, not second couple arm.
Incorrect. Error in proportion between force magnitudes.

questions.topic: Rotational Dynamics - Conservation of Angular Momentum
questions.q: A figure skater spins with angular velocity $\omega_1 = 14\text{ rad/s}$ with arms fully extended. She pulls her arms to her chest, decreasing her moment of inertia by $30\%$. Calculate new angular velocity $\omega_2$.
questions.hint: In absence of external torques, angular momentum is conserved: $I_1 \cdot \omega_1 = I_2 \cdot \omega_2$. If moment of inertia decreases by $30\%$, final value is $I_2 = 0.70 \cdot I_1$.
explanations: Correct! Since $I_2 = (1 - 0.30) I_1 = 0.70 I_1$, from angular momentum conservation $I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2$ we get $\omega_2 = \frac{I_1 \omega_1}{0.70 I_1} = \frac{14}{0.70} = 20\text{ rad/s}$.
Incorrect. $18.2\text{ rad/s}$ obtained incorrectly increasing speed by $30\%$ ($14 \cdot 1.30$).
Incorrect. $9.8\text{ rad/s}$ equals $14 \cdot 0.70$, assuming speed decreases along with moment of inertia.
Incorrect. $28\text{ rad/s}$ assumes halving moment of inertia ($50\%$ instead of $30\%$).
Incorrect. Calculation error in percentage reduction.

questions.topic: Theory of Rotational Dynamics - Moment of Inertia
questions.q: True or False?\nThe moment of inertia $I$ of a rigid body depends only on total mass $M$ and not on how mass is distributed relative to rotation axis.
questions.hint: Think of moment of inertia formula for point mass: $I = m \cdot r^2$.
explanations: Incorrect. Distance of mass from rotation axis plays fundamental role (varies with distance squared $r^2$).
Correct! Moment of inertia strongly depends on mass distribution around rotation axis: farther mass is concentrated from axis, larger $I$ is.

questions.topic: Theory of Rotational Dynamics - Conservation of Angular Momentum
questions.q: True or False?\nIf external net torque acting on a system is zero, angular velocity $\omega$ remains strictly constant, even if body shape changes.
questions.hint: Consider figure skater pulling in arms while spinning.
explanations: Incorrect. In absence of external torques, total angular momentum $L = I \cdot \omega$ is conserved, not angular velocity alone.
Correct! Total angular momentum $L = I \cdot \omega$ is conserved. If system shape changes varying moment of inertia $I$, angular velocity $\omega$ must change inversely.

questions.topic: Theory of Rotational Dynamics - Angular Momentum in Uniform Circular Motion
questions.q: True or False?\nIn uniform circular motion of a particle around origin, angular momentum vector $\vec{L}$ has constant direction in time, orthogonal to motion plane.
questions.hint: Use right-hand rule for cross product $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$.
explanations: Correct! Since position vector $\vec{r}$ and momentum $\vec{p}$ lie in trajectory plane, cross product $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$ is perpendicular to plane and conserves magnitude, direction, and sense.
Incorrect. If motion remains in same plane at constant speed, angular momentum vector direction does not change.

questions.topic: Theory of Rotational Dynamics - Rotational Kinetic Energy
questions.q: True or False?\nRotational kinetic energy of a rigid body rotating around fixed axis is directly proportional to its angular velocity $\omega$.
questions.hint: Compare translational kinetic energy formula $K_{\text{trans}} = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$ with rotational $K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$.
explanations: Incorrect. Rotational kinetic energy does not grow linearly with angular velocity.
Correct! Rotational kinetic energy formula is $K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$, proportional to SQUARE of angular velocity $\omega^2$.

questions.topic: Theory of Rotational Dynamics - Fundamental Equation of Rotation
questions.q: What is Newton's Second Law applied to rotational motion of a rigid body about a fixed axis?
questions.hint: Map translational quantities to rotational counterparts: force $F$ becomes torque $M$, mass $m$ becomes moment of inertia $I$, acceleration $a$ becomes angular acceleration $\alpha$.
explanations: Correct! Total external torque $M$ produces angular acceleration $\alpha$ inversely proportional to moment of inertia $I$ ($M = I \cdot \alpha$).
Incorrect. $I \cdot \omega$ defines angular momentum $L$, not torque $M$.
Incorrect. $M = m \cdot a$ mixes translational and rotational quantities incorrectly.

questions.topic: Theory of Rotational Dynamics - Energy and Angular Momentum Conservation
questions.q: A spinning figure skater pulls arms in, halving her moment of inertia ($I_2 = \frac{1}{2} I_1$). In absence of external friction, what happens to her rotational kinetic energy?
questions.hint: Recall angular momentum $L = I \omega$ is conserved. Express rotational kinetic energy in terms of $L$: $K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{L^2}{2I}$.
explanations: Correct! Since $L$ is constant, angular velocity doubles ($\omega_2 = 2\omega_1$). Substituting into $K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$ gives $K_2 = \frac{1}{2} (\frac{1}{2} I_1) (2\omega_1)^2 = 2 K_1$. Skater's muscular work increased kinetic energy.
Incorrect. Energy increases, not decreases, due to internal work done by skater muscles pulling arms in.
Incorrect. Kinetic energy is not conserved when internal forces do work changing body configuration.

questions.topic: Theory of Rotational Dynamics - Units of Angular Momentum
questions.q: What is the SI unit of angular momentum $L$?
questions.hint: Use vector definition $L = r \cdot p = r \cdot m \cdot v$.
explanations: Correct! Multiplying distance ($\text{m}$) by mass ($\text{kg}$) and speed ($\text{m/s}$), unit is $\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 / \text{s}$ (or $\text{J} \cdot \text{s}$).
Incorrect. $\text{kg} \cdot \text{m} / \text{s}^2$ is definition of Newton ($\text{N}$), unit of force.
Incorrect. $\text{N} \cdot \text{m}$ is unit of torque or work/energy (Joule).

questions.topic: Theory of Rotational Dynamics - Moment of Inertia of Geometric Objects
questions.q: Two cylinders have same mass $M$ and outer radius $R$. First is solid homogeneous cylinder ($I_1 = \frac{1}{2} M R^2$), second is thin hollow cylinder ($I_2 = M R^2$). Which presents greater resistance to changing rotation state?
questions.hint: Moment of inertia quantifies rotational inertia: larger $I$ means greater resistance to rotation changes.
options: Both offer exactly the same resistance
explanations: Correct! Hollow cylinder has double moment of inertia ($I_2 = M R^2 > \frac{1}{2} M R^2 = I_1$) because all mass is at maximum distance $R$ from axis, offering greater rotational resistance.
Incorrect. Solid cylinder has mass distribution closer to central axis, making moment of inertia smaller and easier to rotate.
Incorrect. Although having same mass and radius, different geometric mass distributions make moments of inertia and rotational responses distinctly different.
